title: Model cards compared, pack 2: what frontier developers’ cards disclose
status: Candidate research pack outside application data. passages.quote: Update (June 20, 2024): We have added an addendum covering Claude 3.5 Sonnet.

cells.question: Q02

passages.quote: Developed by Anthropic and announced in March 2024, the Claude 3 model family will be available in our consumer offerings (Claude.ai, Claude Pro) as well as enterprise solutions like the Anthropic API, Amazon Bedrock, and Google Vertex AI.

cells.note: The card gives the forms of availability (consumer products, the API and two cloud platforms) and the month of announcement, March 2024. It gives no release or availability date; an announcement month is a different event.

search.read: Sections 1–2 and term search across PDF pp. 1–42.

cells.question: Q03

passages.quote: Anthropic, “Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy.” September, 2023.

passages.locator: Section 6.2.1 'Autonomous Replication and Adaption (ARA) evaluations', PDF p. 24
passages.quote: The evaluation tasks were based on tasks defined in the appendix of v1.0 of our RSP [5]

cells.note: The card names the Responsible Scaling Policy and identifies the edition by its date (September 2023) and as v1.0 (rsp-2023).

cells.question: Q04

passages.quote: September, 2023. https://www.anthropic.com/index/anthropics-responsible-scaling-policy.

cells.note: The card gives a bibliographic reference with an address. The address is Anthropic's announcement page for the policy, not the policy PDF.

cells.question: Q05

passages.quote: Our results show no indicators of catastrophic risk, and therefore we classify all of our Claude 3 models as ASL-2.

cells.note: The card assigns ASL-2 to all three Claude 3 models. It states that the evaluations were run on a lower-refusal version of Claude 3 Opus.

cells.question: Q06

passages.locator: Section 6.3 'Security and Deployment Mitigations', PDF p. 26
passages.quote: we still take various precautionary measures at ASL-2. We harden security against opportunistic attackers for all copies of Claude 3 model weights.

passages.locator: Section 6.3 'Security and Deployment Mitigations', PDF p. 26
passages.quote: You can read a more detailed description of our ASL-2 security and deployment measures in our full policy [5].

cells.note: The card states security and deployment measures at ASL-2, the level assigned in Q05, including automated detection of CBRN- and cyber-related prompts. This is the developer's account of the measures.

cells.question: Q07

passages.quote: In summary, the model did not meet our most conservative biological risk thresholds, and our expert consultants agreed.

cells.note: The card states biological evaluations (automated question sets and a human uplift trial) with the outcome that the early-indicator thresholds were not met. No chemical, radiological or nuclear evaluation is reported for Claude 3. Evaluation details are not recorded (hazard rule).

cells.question: Q08

passages.quote: We judged that the model did not pass the ASL-3 threshold on any of the early indicator tests.

cells.note: The card states cyber evaluations (vulnerability discovery and exploit development) with the outcome that the ASL-3 threshold was not passed. Scores and task details are not recorded (hazard rule).

cells.question: Q09

passages.locator: Section 6.2.1 'Autonomous Replication and Adaption (ARA) evaluations', PDF p. 24
passages.quote: Across all the rounds, the model was clearly below our ARA ASL-3 risk threshold, having failed at least 3 out of 5 tasks

cells.note: The card states autonomous replication and adaptation evaluations with the outcome that the ASL-3 warning threshold was not crossed. Task contents are not recorded (hazard rule).

cells.question: Q10
cells.note: No report of an evaluation of persuasive or manipulative capability was found in the Claude 3 card (PDF pp. 1–42).

search.read: Sections 5.4, 6 and 7 (PDF pp. 10–31) and term search across PDF pp. 1–42.

setAside.reason: Describes testing of responses to election misinformation prompts, which concerns misuse, not the model's persuasive capability.

cells.question: Q11

passages.locator: Section 6.2.1 'Autonomous Replication and Adaption (ARA) evaluations', PDF p. 24
passages.quote: These tasks are selected to indicate whether the model can make meaningful progress towards accumulating resources, exploiting software security vulnerabilities, deceiving humans, and surviving autonomously in the absence of human intervention to stop the model.

passages.locator: Section 6.2.1 'Autonomous Replication and Adaption (ARA) evaluations', PDF p. 24
passages.quote: Our pre-specified warning indicator for ASL-3 was the model passing 50% or more of the tasks (described below) with at least a 10% pass rate (i.e., succeeding at one in ten attempts) – the model did not cross this threshold.

cells.note: The ARA evaluations are described as indicating, among other capabilities, whether the model can make progress at deceiving humans, and the card gives one combined conclusion for them: the ASL-3 warning indicator was not crossed. It gives no conclusion on deception separately, and reports no evaluation of the model’s own propensity for deception, scheming or sabotage. The same evaluations are recorded under Q09. Task contents are not recorded (hazard rule).

search.read: Sections 5.4–5.7, 6 and 7 (PDF pp. 10–31) and term search across PDF pp. 1–42.

setAside.reason: An honesty benchmark of factual accuracy, not an evaluation of deception or scheming.

crossFamily.result: material disagreement, applied: the checker reads partly (blind), because Q11 includes capability for deception and the ARA scope includes deceiving humans, with a combined conclusion. The pack had read not found, setting the passage aside as a Q09 evaluation; the criterion makes no such exclusion. The preparer accepts the checker’s reading.

cells.note: The card reports no cyber-offence evaluation; it refers to the CWM Preparedness Report.

setAside.reason: SWE-bench and coding benchmarks are product benchmarks.

cells.question: Q09
cells.note: No evaluation of autonomy, self-replication, self-improvement or AI research and development was found.

setAside.reason: SWE-bench Verified is reported as product capability; agentic task benchmarks of this kind do not meet the criterion.

cells.question: Q10
cells.note: No evaluation of persuasion or manipulation was found.

cells.question: Q11
cells.note: No evaluation of deception, scheming, sabotage or undermining oversight was found.

cells.question: Q12
cells.note: No testing described as red-teaming was found.

cells.question: Q13
cells.note: No external tester is named or described.

cells.question: Q14
cells.note: No government body is named.

cells.question: Q15

passages.quote: To ensure responsible release, we have conducted an assessment of CWM’s capabilities across a range of potential threats

cells.note: The card states the release and an assessment conducted for it, in the first person plural. It does not describe a decision to release or name who made one.

cells.question: Q16

passages.quote: Although we have performed some limited evaluations, we have not conducted a full range of possible evaluations for these models.

cells.note: The card states that its evaluations are limited, that performance in production and real-world use has not been evaluated, and that the model has not been fully evaluated for content risks.

cells.question: Q01

passages.quote: Date: June 12, 2026

cells.note: The report prints the date June 12, 2026, without a kind. arXiv's margin stamp on PDF p. 1 reads '14 May 2026', which does not agree with the printed date or with the identifier 2606.12429; both are recorded as read, and neither is the card's own statement of publication. Meta’s own copies were retrieved in the cross-family check of 2026-11-04 (not here: ai.meta.com answered HTTP 400 and web.archive.org refused connections): an Internet Archive capture of 2026-04-14 holds an earlier 158-page expression that prints April 14, 2026, and the live copy prints May 26, 2026. Under 3a the row is dated by that earliest located copy, 2026-04-14; the arXiv copy read here is a later expression. The arXiv stamp of 14 May is the submission date, corroborated by the repository history.

cells.question: Q02

passages.quote: We therefore release Muse Spark as the underlying model of Meta AI.
early checkpoints of Muse Spark were initially deployed to a small, percentage-limited subset of product users prior to broad availability.

cells.note: The report gives the release form (the model underlying Meta AI) and a sequence of controlled deployments before broad availability. It gives no release or availability date.

search.read: Abstract, Sections 1–1.3 and term search across the report.

cells.question: Q03

passages.quote: https://ai.meta.com/static-resource/Meta_Advanced-AI-Scaling-Framework-v2
Muse Spark was developed and evaluated under Meta’s Advanced AI Scaling Framework

cells.note: The report names the Advanced AI Scaling Framework and gives an address whose file name names version 2 (meta-aasf-v2-0). The text gives no version number of its own.

cells.question: Q04

passages.quote: https://ai.meta.com/static-resource/Meta_Advanced-AI-Scaling-Framework-v2

cells.note: The report gives the framework's address in a footnote.

cells.question: Q05

passages.quote: we determined the model, prior to applying mitigations, falls under the “high risk” threshold under the Advanced AI Scaling Framework
However, after applying mitigations, the residual risk of the model is that of “moderate or lower risk.”

cells.note: The report states a 'high risk' determination before mitigations, for the chemical and biological category, and a residual 'moderate or lower risk' after mitigations. It states 'moderate or lower' for cybersecurity and loss of control (Q08, Q09).

cells.question: Q06

passages.quote: In response to the “high risk” determination, we have defined, implemented, and validated a set of mitigations to reduce the residual risk of public deployment to “moderate or lower.”

cells.note: The report ties mitigations (refusal mechanisms, detection of persistent malicious use and monitoring) to the 'high risk' determination, and states that deployment is conditional on them under the framework. It also states cyber-misuse monitoring as a compensating control. This is the developer's account, not evidence that the mitigations work.

cells.question: Q07

passages.quote: assess that the model has “high risk” for Chemical and/or Biological risks.

cells.note: The report states chemical and biological evaluations (dual-use knowledge, agentic scientific tasks and high-risk bottlenecks) with the outcome 'high risk' before mitigations and 'moderate or lower' residual risk after them. Evaluation details are not recorded (hazard rule).

cells.question: Q08

passages.quote: We assess cybersecurity risk as “moderate or lower” with respect to the threat scenarios outlined in Meta’s Advanced AI Scaling Framework.

cells.note: The report states knowledge, capture-the-flag, real-world and social-engineering cyber evaluations with the framework outcome 'moderate or lower'. Scores are not recorded (hazard rule).

cells.question: Q09

passages.locator: Section 1.1.1, 'Loss of Control risks', PDF p. 9
passages.quote: We assess loss of control risk as “moderate or lower”.

passages.locator: Section 1.1.1, 'Loss of Control risks', PDF p. 10
passages.quote: Its autonomous technical capabilities—spanning software engineering, ML engineering, and end-to-end research—remain too constrained

cells.note: The report states loss-of-control evaluations, including acceleration of AI development, with the outcome 'moderate or lower' and the conclusion that autonomous research capabilities remain constrained.

cells.question: Q10

passages.quote: we have included results from an evaluation developed by Charlemagne Labs that specifically measures social engineering capabilities in multi-turn settings.
we do not find the capabilities of the model (without system level guardrails) to be sufficiently high to trigger a determination of high risk according to our Advanced AI Scaling Framework

cells.note: The report states a multi-turn social-engineering capability evaluation (an attacker model trying to convince a simulated victim), with composite scores against open models (Figure 20), as part of the cyber domain, and concludes that the capability is not high enough to trigger a high-risk determination under its framework. The victims are simulated: no result with human subjects is reported. Methods are not recorded (hazard rule).

setAside.reason: 'Refusals: Social Engineering' measures refusal of misuse requests, not capability.

crossFamily.result: material disagreement, applied: the checker reads stated (blind), because section 2.2.2.3 gives a conclusion for the social-engineering evaluation (PDF p. 48), and Q10 asks for a conclusion, not a risk category specific to persuasion. The pack had read partly. The preparer accepts the checker’s reading, keeping the simulated-victim and cyber-domain limits.

cells.question: Q11

passages.locator: Section 1.1.1, 'Loss of Control risks', PDF p. 10
passages.quote: The model demonstrates contained deception and exhibits some propensities toward agentic misalignment in controlled settings, such as self-preservation and resistance to discontinuation.

passages.locator: Section 1.1.1, 'Loss of Control risks', PDF p. 10
passages.quote: These behaviors remain within acceptable thresholds but warrant monitoring for loss of control risks.

cells.note: The report states evaluations of deception, agentic misalignment, sandbagging, monitor evasion and alignment faking, with the conclusion quoted. It reports Apollo Research's finding of high evaluation awareness and its own follow-up (Section 4.1.11).

cells.question: Q12

passages.quote: A third-party human red team from HandshakeAI32 was granted pre-release access to a few versions of Muse Spark and Meta AI Thinking to manually evaluate robustness against jailbreak attacks.
HandshakeAI prioritized four categories: (1) sex-related crimes, (2) violent crimes, (3) non-violent crimes, and (4) self-harm and suicide.
HandshakeAI reported approximately 149 hours of red-teaming effort

cells.note: The report states third-party human red teaming of jailbreak robustness with pre-release access, with its scope: four prioritised content-policy categories and approximately 149 hours of effort (hours of effort, not a testing period). It also reports large-scale automated red teaming (Section 3.1). No number of testers is given in the passage read. The “32” after HandshakeAI in the first quotation is a footnote marker.

crossFamily.result: minor, applied: the scope given in the same paragraph (four prioritised categories, about 149 hours of effort) is added.

cells.question: Q13

passages.quote: Independent third-party testing by Apollo Research found Muse Spark has the highest rate of evaluation awareness they have observed to date.

cells.note: The report names Apollo Research (evaluation awareness), HandshakeAI (human red teaming, Q12) and Charlemagne Labs (social engineering, Q10), and names Deloitte, Faculty, Frontier Design and SecureBio as engaged in the chemical and biological assessment (Section 2.1).

cells.question: Q14
cells.note: No government body is named as having tested or received access to Muse Spark.

search.read: Abstract, Sections 1–2.2 and term search across the report.

setAside.reason: Names UK AISI and CAISI as users of a benchmark in their own testing, not as testing this model.

cells.question: Q15

passages.quote: We then describe the governance process that led to the decision to deploy Muse Spark under Meta’s Advanced AI Scaling Framework2
Key decision-makers for Muse Spark’s risk threshold determinations were the Chief AI Officer and Director of Alignment and Risk

cells.note: The report refers to 'the decision to deploy' and 'our launch decision' in the company's voice, and names the Chief AI Officer and the Director of Alignment and Risk as the decision-makers for the risk-threshold determinations. It does not name a maker of the deployment decision other than the company.

cells.question: Q16

passages.quote: We cannot rule out this possibility on the basis of behavioral evaluations alone and flag it as an inherent epistemic limitation of assessments of this kind.

cells.note: The report states that a model capable of strategic behaviour could make its evaluations appear credible, and that this cannot be ruled out by behavioural evaluations. It also states that some baseline assessments give only a lower bound on performance and that evaluation awareness qualifies some results.

cells.question: Q01

passages.quote: GPT-4o System Card OpenAI∗ August 8, 2024

cells.note: The card prints the date August 8, 2024 under its title. No revision date is printed.

cells.question: Q02

passages.quote: Following the text output only deployment of GPT-4o, we worked with independent third party labs, METR and Apollo Research
At the time of writing, external red teaming of the GPT-4o API is ongoing.

cells.note: The card refers to a text-output-only deployment, to the API and to advanced voice mode in the iOS app used in red teaming (Phase 4), as relative timing and forms. It gives no release or availability date.

search.read: Sections 1–3.1 and 4 and term search across the card.

cells.question: Q03

passages.quote: We evaluated GPT-4o in accordance with our Preparedness Framework[4].
OpenAI, “Openai preparedness framework beta,” 2023.

cells.note: The card names the Preparedness Framework and identifies the edition in reference [4] as the beta of 2023 (preparedness-beta-2023).

crossFamily.result: minor, applied: the reference quotation is repaired. The default PDF text layer interleaves the address with the title; the printed reference reads as now quoted (checked by the checker visually, and here against pdftotext’s raw reading order). Identification as the 2023 beta is unchanged.

cells.question: Q04

passages.quote: Openai preparedness framework openai-preparedness-framework-beta.pdf. beta,” 2023. https://cdn.openai.com/

cells.note: The card gives a bibliographic reference to the framework with an address on cdn.openai.com and the file name of the beta framework. In the text layer the address and the file name are separated by the title.

cells.question: Q05

passages.quote: the Safety Advisory Group recommended classifying GPT-4o before mitigations as borderline medium risk for persuasion, and low risk in all others.
Therefore, the overall risk score for GPT-4o is classified as medium.

cells.note: The card states a pre-mitigation classification in the framework's categories (persuasion borderline medium; cybersecurity, CBRN and model autonomy low) and an overall medium score, on the Safety Advisory Group's recommendation.

cells.question: Q06

passages.quote: If a model passes a high risk threshold, we do not deploy the model until mitigations lower the score to medium.

passages.locator: Section 3.3 'Observed safety challenges, evaluations and mitigations', PDF p. 5
passages.quote: integrated classifiers for blocking specific generations as a part of the deployed system

cells.note: The card states the framework's deployment condition and, for the voice risks in Section 3.3, mitigations such as post-training and output classifiers. It does not tie any mitigation to the medium classification in Q05. This is the developer's account of the mitigations.

search.read: Sections 3.3–3.8 and 6 and term search across the card.

cells.question: Q07

passages.locator: Section 3.6 'Biological threats', Preparedness Scorecard, PDF p. 14
passages.quote: Biological Threats Score: Low GPT-4o does not advance biological threat creation capabilities sufficient to meet our medium risk threshold.

cells.note: The card states biological threat evaluations with a low score under the framework. The framework category is CBRN; no separate chemical, radiological or nuclear result is reported. Evaluation details are not recorded (hazard rule).

cells.question: Q08

passages.quote: GPT-4o does not advance real world vulnerability exploitation capabilities sufficient to meet our medium risk threshold.

cells.note: The card states capture-the-flag evaluations with a low cybersecurity score. Task-level results are not recorded (hazard rule).

cells.question: Q09

passages.locator: Section 3.8 'Model autonomy', Preparedness Scorecard, PDF p. 17
passages.quote: GPT-4o does not advance self-exfiltration, self-improvement, or resource acquisition capabilities sufficient to meet our medium risk threshold.

cells.note: The card states model-autonomy evaluations with a low score. Section 4.1 adds METR's assessment of autonomous capabilities, which the card reports as finding no significant increase over GPT-4.

cells.question: Q10

passages.quote: Based on pre-registered thresholds, the voice modality was classified as low risk, while the text modality marginally crossed into medium risk.

cells.note: The card states persuasion evaluations of text and voice, with a medium score for text and low for voice.

cells.question: Q11

passages.quote: Based on these findings, Apollo Research believes that it is unlikely that GPT-4o is capable of catastrophic scheming.

cells.note: The card reports Apollo Research's evaluation of capabilities related to scheming (self-knowledge, theory of mind, self-reasoning, alignment faking), with Apollo's conclusion. It concerns capability, not propensity.

cells.question: Q12

passages.quote: OpenAI worked with more than 100 external red teamers2 , speaking a total of 45 different languages, and representing geographic backgrounds of 29 different countries.
starting in early March and continuing through late June 2024.

cells.note: The card states external red teaming in four phases, with the number of testers, languages and countries, the period, and the categories covered (disallowed content, mis/disinformation, bias and others).

cells.question: Q13

passages.quote: we worked with independent third party labs, METR and Apollo Research to add an additional layer of validation for key risks from general autonomous capabilities.

cells.note: The card names METR and Apollo Research as having assessed the model after its text-output deployment. Section 3.6 names Gryphon Scientific as having helped design the biological questions and rubrics, not as having tested the model.

cells.question: Q14
cells.note: No government body is named as having tested or received access to GPT-4o.

search.read: Sections 3–6 and term search across the card.

setAside.reason: 'UK AISI’s Theory of Mind' names a task used by Apollo Research, not testing of the model by the institute.
Refers to voluntary commitments to the White House, not testing.

cells.question: Q15

passages.quote: the Safety Advisory Group recommended classifying GPT-4o before mitigations as borderline medium risk for persuasion, and low risk in all others.
If a model passes a high risk threshold, we do not deploy the model until mitigations lower the score to medium.

cells.note: The card names the Safety Advisory Group for the risk classification and states the framework's deployment condition. It refers to the model's deployment but does not describe a decision to release it or name who made one.

search.read: Sections 2–4 and 6 and term search across the card.

setAside.reason: 'Deployment preparation was carried out via …' describes preparation, which alone is not a release decision (decision 13a).

cells.question: Q16

passages.locator: Section 3.2 'Evaluation methodology', 'Limitations of the evaluation methodology', PDF p. 4
passages.quote: First, the validity of this evaluation format depends on the capability and reliability of the TTS model.

cells.note: The card states limits of its audio evaluation method, which converts text evaluations to speech: some inputs are unsuitable for conversion and the conversion may be lossy.

cells.question: Q01

passages.quote: Grok 4 Model Card xAI Last updated: August 20, 2025

cells.note: The card prints only a last-updated date (August 20, 2025), not a publication date. The file name carries the same date.

search.read: Cover and term search across the card.

cells.question: Q02

passages.quote: xAI deploys Grok 4 in both the consumer-facing applications (Grok 4 Web) and through an enterprise use-focused API (Grok 4 API).
We report evaluations for Grok 4 API and Grok 4 Web now available to our customers, including in the EU.

cells.note: The card gives the forms of availability (consumer applications and an API, including in the EU), in the present tense, with no release date.

search.read: Sections 1 and 3 and term search across the card.

cells.question: Q03

passages.quote: Following our Risk Management Framework (RMF), we aim to reduce the risk of severe, large-scale harms to people, property, and society from AI.

cells.note: The card names xAI's Risk Management Framework without an edition. The RMF is not among the dataset's framework editions (5a); see frameworkEditionNote.

cells.question: Q04

passages.quote: we filter for detailed information or substantial assistance regarding the critical steps identified in Section 2 of our RMF.

cells.note: The card refers to a section of the framework as a document, without an address or bibliographic reference. The reference list does not include the RMF.

search.read: Whole card, references and link annotations.

cells.question: Q05
cells.note: No outcome in the framework's own categories (a threshold reached, not reached or not ruled out) was found. The card organises its evaluations by the RMF's two risk categories and states an overall conclusion outside threshold language.

search.read: Sections 1–2 and term search across the card.

setAside.reason: 'we believe that Grok 4 overall presents a low risk for malicious use and loss of control' is a conclusion after mitigations; the card does not present it as a level or threshold of the framework.

cells.question: Q06

passages.quote: Due to Grok 4’s strong dual-use biological capabilities, we have deployed narrow, topically-focused filters across all product surfaces as an additional safeguard against bioweapons-related abuse.

cells.note: The card ties biological and chemical filters to its capability results and to steps identified in the RMF, not to a framework determination (none is stated, Q05). It also states a refusal policy, a system prompt and input filters (Section 2.1.3). This is the developer's account of the safeguards.

cells.question: Q07

passages.quote: The area of highest concern is Grok 4's expert-level biology capabilities, which significantly exceed human expert baselines.
We do not evaluate radiological or nuclear capabilities.

cells.note: The card states biology and chemistry dual-use knowledge evaluations, with the conclusion that biology is the area of highest concern and with a separate finding on chemistry knowledge; it states that radiological and nuclear capabilities are not evaluated. No threshold language. Scores are not recorded (hazard rule).

cells.question: Q08

passages.quote: third-party testing shows that Grok 4’s end-to-end offensive cyber capabilities remain below the level of a human professional.

cells.note: The card states cyber knowledge and agentic capture-the-flag evaluations and a conclusion relative to human professionals, attributed to third-party testing. No threshold language. Scores are not recorded (hazard rule).

cells.question: Q09
cells.note: No evaluation of autonomy, self-replication, self-improvement or AI research and development was found. The card's loss-of-control category is assessed through propensities (Q11).

setAside.reason: A rogue AI exfiltrating its weights is given as an example risk scenario, not as an evaluation.

cells.question: Q10

passages.quote: We measure persuasion with OpenAI’s MakeMeSay evaluation, where an attacker model attempts to manipulate a defender model to say a codeword

cells.note: The card reports a persuasion evaluation and a win rate in Table 3, with no stated conclusion about persuasive capability.

setAside.reason: The 'Manipulation' row of Table 2 reports sycophancy, recorded under Q11.

cells.question: Q11

passages.quote: We find that our system prompt mitigation makes the model less willing to contradict its beliefs, thus lowering the lying rate.

cells.note: The card reports deception (lying under pressure), sycophancy and political-bias evaluations as 'concerning propensities', with the conclusion quoted. No scheming, sabotage or oversight evaluation was found.

cells.question: Q12
cells.note: No testing described as red-teaming was found. The card reports adversarial robustness evaluations (jailbreaks, prompt injection) without calling them red-teaming.

setAside.reason: Jailbreak attacks on a query set are an evaluation setting, not described as red-teaming.

cells.question: Q13

passages.quote: third-party testing shows that Grok 4’s end-to-end offensive cyber capabilities remain below the level of a human professional.

cells.note: The card refers to third-party cyber testing without naming the third party.

setAside.reason: 'data produced by third-parties for xAI' concerns training data, not testing.

cells.question: Q14
cells.note: No government body is named as having tested or received access to Grok 4.

setAside.reason: 'the open-source Inspect evaluation framework developed by the UK AISI' names a tool, not testing by the institute.
DoE and DoD are named as restricting nuclear information, not as testing the model.

cells.question: Q15
cells.note: No statement that a release or deployment decision was made was found.

setAside.reason: States deployment and availability; availability alone is not a decision to release (decision 13a).
'we believe that Grok 4 overall presents a low risk for malicious use and loss of control' is a risk conclusion, not tied by the card to a release; no maker of a release decision is named.
'we assess that Grok’s enforcement of our basic refusal policy is sufficient' is a safeguards assessment for cyber risks, not tied by the card to a release.

cells.question: Q16

passages.quote: Note that these evaluations measure dual-use knowledge: a high score indicates greater capability to enable weapons development, not necessarily increased risk.
For all datasets, we only assess performance on text-only questions.

cells.note: The card states that its dual-use evaluations measure knowledge rather than risk, and that only text-only questions are assessed.
